sections.title: The Mitzvot of Orla and Neta Revai
sections.html:
It is a mitzva not to derive benefit from orla fruit, which is the fruit growing in the first three years of a tree, and it is a mitzva to bring the fruit growing in the fourth year up to Jerusalem and to eat it in holiness and in praise of God, and through this blessing will be drawn to the fruit that will grow from the fifth year onward. As it is stated (Vayikra 19:23-25): "And when you come into the land and plant any tree for food, you shall treat its fruit as forbidden (lit. 'uncircumcised'); three years it shall be forbidden to you, it shall not be eaten. And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, for giving praise to the Lord. And in the fifth year you may eat its fruit, so that it may increase its yield for you; I am the Lord your God."

'Orla' means being sealed. Therefore, one of 'uncircumcised heart' (Yeḥezkel 44:9) is one whose heart is sealed; one of 'uncircumcised ears' (Yirmiyahu 6:10) is one whose ears are sealed from hearing; and one of 'uncircumcised lips' (Shemot 6:12) is a person whose lips are sealed from speaking. Thus we were commanded that the fruit of the first three years be sealed off to us, that we not eat it and not derive benefit from it (Rashi and Rashbam, Vayikra there).

On the day the Children of Israel crossed the Jordan in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun and entered the Land, they became obligated in the mitzva of orla, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23): "And when you come into the land and plant." And even a tree that a gentile planted in his field from then on is obligated in orla and its fruit is forbidden to us for benefit, as it is stated (there): "any tree for food" – to include a tree that a gentile planted (Torat Kohanim there).

Outside the Land, the law of orla applies as a 'halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai' (a law transmitted to Moshe at Sinai), and the halakha established that it applies only when there is certainty that the fruit is orla; but whenever there is a doubt about it, even though it is very likely that the fruit is orla, there is no prohibition in it, for doubtful orla in the Land is forbidden, and outside the Land it is permitted (Mishna and Yerushalmi, Orla 3:7; Bavli Kiddushin 39a; SA 294:8; below, section 11). The borders of the Land with regard to the mitzva of orla are the borders of those who came up from Egypt. And even according to those who hold that the southern Arava is outside the border of those who came up from Egypt, since it is under the rule of the State of Israel, the mitzva applies to it by Torah law (below 12:2, n. 2; 17).1

Whether one plants a seed or plants a cutting, from the time they take root in the ground one begins to count three years for them (section 4 will explain how the years are calculated).

sections.title: The Reason for the Mitzva
sections.html:
The reason for the mitzva is to honor God with the first fruits of the tree, to eat them in holiness in Jerusalem and to praise God through them for all the good He has granted us. And since generally the fruits growing in the first three years are not plentiful and choice, it is not fitting to praise God with them, and therefore the Torah forbade them, so that the beginning of our eating will be in holiness and in praise of God in the fourth year, when many good fruits already grow. And through this, the pleasantness of God and His blessing will rest upon the fruits growing in all the years, and eating them will be connected to faith and will grant vitality to add goodness and blessing in the world. Similarly, the Torah commanded to sanctify the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals and the bikkurim (first fruits). And such is also the reason of the mitzvot of ḥadash, teruma, ḥalla and the first shearing (see Ramban, Vayikra there; Ḥinukh 246-247).

We further learn from this mitzva the value of self-restraint, which is very important and beneficial. The ability to restrain oneself and to defer the satisfaction of desire to the appropriate time is a necessary condition for a person's success in this world and in the World to Come. For example, it is known that a person who studies diligently in his youth will be more successful in his personal life and in his livelihood, and nevertheless many young people do not succeed in restraining themselves, are drawn after their impulses and waste their time on various amusements. Likewise, it is known that dating relationships between young men and women not for the sake of marriage harm their ability to marry and to establish a faithful home with love, and nevertheless many do not succeed in restraining themselves, and are drawn after their impulses into stormy relationships that do not lead to a true covenant. And likewise there are people who do not succeed in restraining themselves from wasting their money on luxuries, such as buying an apartment more expensive than they can afford, and do not succeed in saving money
to help their children acquire a profession and marry, and to support themselves in their old age. Adam, the first man, too, was drawn after his impulse and sinned because he did not restrain himself from eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, and thereby brought death upon himself and his descendants. Through the mitzva of orla, a person learns to see his fruits growing and to refrain from benefiting from them, and in this way he learns to overcome his impulse and to restrain himself. This is what the Sages said (Vayikra Rabba 25:2): "Who will remove the dust from your eyes, Adam, the first man, for you could not stand by your commandment for a single hour, and behold, your children wait for orla three years" (see Beitza 25b).

The Sages further said that the fruits of the first years express a desire to come into actuality before the proper time, without the appropriate restraint, and therefore they have no completeness and impurity clings to them. The fruits of the first three years correspond to the three evil and hard kelipot (husks), which seal and conceal the light. And the fourth year corresponds to the thin kelipa in which good and evil are mixed, and its fruits are rectified by bringing them up to Jerusalem and eating them in holiness (Zohar vol. 3, 87a; Sha'arei Ora, Gate 5; Pardes Rimonim, Gate 25:7).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Prohibition of Benefit
sections.html:
The fruits growing in the first three years are forbidden to eat and to derive benefit from. Therefore, it is forbidden to light a lamp with oil from orla fruit, and it is forbidden to heat an oven with orla fruit. Likewise, it is forbidden to place orla fruit in the ground for the purpose of fertilizing, but it is permitted to throw them on the ground without intending to fertilize. Even for the sake of a mitzva it is forbidden to use orla fruit; therefore, an etrog of orla is invalid for the four species on Sukkot (Sukka 34b; SA YD 294:24; Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 4:12). Likewise, it is forbidden to benefit from the scent of orla fruit (SA 108:7).2

Likewise, it is forbidden to dye a garment with dye produced from orla fruit. And the garment that was dyed with orla fruit is forbidden for benefit, and so that people will not stumble with it, it must be burned (Yerushalmi Orla 3:1; Bavli Kiddushin 56b). And whenever there is a concern that people will come to benefit from orla fruit, it is a mitzva to burn them or destroy them in another way that will prevent the possibility of benefiting from them. And if possible, it is good to remove the blossoms or the fruits from the tree while they are still small, so that people will not stumble with them.3

Everything that grows with the fruit is forbidden for benefit, including the fruit's seeds and peel, as well as juice that comes out of it. But the tree, its leaves and its blossoms are permitted for benefit. Likewise, the fruit while still very small, to the point that it is not considered a fruit and is called semadar (blossom-stage fruit) – is permitted for benefit. But once it reaches the stage of boser (unripe fruit), even though it is not yet fit for eating, it is already considered a fruit and the prohibition of orla applies to it (Mishna Orla 1:7-9; SA 294:1-2).4

It is forbidden to sow the seeds of orla fruit, and likewise it is forbidden to place an orla fruit in the ground so that a tree will grow from it. But it is permitted to plant a branch of an orla tree, since there is no prohibition of benefit in the tree (Mishna Orla 1:9). If one transgressed and planted an orla fruit, the tree that grows is permitted for benefit, for we hold the rule: "Zeh ve-zeh gorem – mutar" (when both this and that cause it, it is permitted). That is, when there are two causes for the tree's growth – the forbidden fruit and the permitted soil – the tree that grows is permitted for benefit (SA 294:12).

The prohibition of orla also applies to a gentile's tree, whose fruits are forbidden to a Jew for benefit. However, a gentile is permitted to benefit from orla fruit that grew on his own tree or on a Jew's tree, for the prohibition of orla applies to Jews and not to gentiles. But since the fruits are forbidden to a Jew for benefit, a Jew is forbidden to sell his orla fruit to a gentile, and likewise he is forbidden to give them as a gift to a gentile or even to feed them to a wild animal, for in this way too the Jew benefits from them (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:16).

However, before the orla fruits have begun to grow, it is permitted to sell them to a gentile, for since the Jew receives the money even before the fruits have come into the world, he does not benefit from the fruits but from the tree, which he is selling, and the tree is permitted for benefit (SA 294:15; Nekudot Ha-kesef there). And this is on condition that there is no concern that the gentile will sell the orla fruit to a Jew and cause him to stumble in a prohibition, for example, where the gentile sells them in a place where there are no Jews.

sections.title: Calculating the Years of Orla
sections.html:
In counting the years of orla we take into account two dates: the 1st of Tishrei, which is the New Year for years and for plantings, and Tu Bi-Shvat (the 15th of Shevat), which is the New Year for trees; this is because any fruit that buds by Tu Bi-Shvat certainly budded by the power of the rains that the tree received in the previous year. We have another rule: thirty days in a year are considered a year (Rosh Hashana 9b-10b).

This is the calculation: If the tree took root in the ground by the 29th of Av, then by the 1st of Tishrei thirty days will have passed for it, and those thirty days will be counted for it as a full year. Afterward one must wait another two years until the completion of the three years, and since the New Year for trees is Tu Bi-Shvat, one must wait until Tu Bi-Shvat, for the fruits that bud before Tu Bi-Shvat budded by the power of the previous year's rains, when the tree was still orla. Thus, if the tree took root on the 29th of Av 5781, all the fruits that bud on it until Tu Bi-Shvat of the year 5784 will be orla. And all that bud on it from Tu Bi-Shvat 5784 until Tu Bi-Shvat 5785 will be neta revai (fourth-year fruit), and all the fruits that bud on it from Tu Bi-Shvat 5785 will be ḥullin (ordinary, unsanctified). Thus, in practice the law of orla will apply to it for two years and five and a half months.

The Sages estimated that after fourteen days the seed or the cutting takes root in the ground. It emerges that in order for the tree to take root in the ground by the 29th of Av and gain a year, one must plant it at the latest on the 15th of Av. And if one planted a seedling with its clod of earth, there is no need to wait fourteen days, for from the time it is placed in the ground it is considered rooted in it. Consequently, if it is placed in the ground by the 29th of Av, a year is gained.

But if the tree took root in the ground from the 30th of Av 5781 onward, since it did not have thirty days in the year 5781, one begins to count the first year for it only on the 1st of Tishrei 5782, and one will need to wait three full years until the 1st of Tishrei 5785; and since the New Year for trees is Tu Bi-Shvat, one will need to wait several more months for it until Tu Bi-Shvat 5785, and only then will the law of orla depart from the tree. Thus, if the tree took root in the ground on the 30th of Av 5781, the law of orla applies to it for three years and five and a half months. And indeed, there are lenient authorities who hold that the law of orla never lasts more than three years; however, since the law of orla is by Torah law, the halakha follows the stringent opinion.5

sections.title: A Tree That Was Uprooted or Cut Down
sections.html:
A tree that was uprooted from its place, if it still has one root left that connects it to the ground, and its thickness is at least that of the needle with which weavers would stretch the garment, may be reburied in the ground and it is exempt from orla, since it can survive with difficulty through this root. And if not even such a root remains, when it is buried in the ground it becomes obligated in orla again (SA 294:20).

A tree that was uprooted by the wind or swept away by a river, and a clod of earth remained attached to its roots: even though it has no root at all connecting it to the ground, if the tree can live for fourteen days from the clod of earth attached to its roots, it may be reburied in the ground and there is no need to count years of orla for it again. And if it cannot live from it for fourteen days, when it is buried in the ground one will need to count the years of orla for it anew. Therefore, when there is a need to move a fruit tree from place to place, one must be careful to uproot it with a clod of earth in which it can live for fourteen days, and in this way one will not need to count years of orla for it from the beginning. And it is good to prune it beforehand as much as possible, for in this way it survives easily for a long time.6

A tree that was cut down or broken, if any amount of its trunk remains above the ground, it is exempt from orla; and if it was cut down entirely and grew again from its root, it is obligated in orla.7

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Havrakha (Layering) and the Law of Suckers
sections.html:
To create a 'havrakha' (layering), one bends a branch of a developed tree and buries its middle in the ground, and its tip emerges at the place where one wishes to create an additional tree. At first the havrakha tree draws its vitality from the original tree, and over time the part buried in the ground develops roots, and they too nourish the new tree. Regarding orla, as long as the new tree draws vitality from the original tree, even if most of its vitality comes from the roots of the havrakha, it is drawn after the original tree and is exempt from orla. And even if from the second tree they layered a third tree, and from the third they layered a fourth tree, as long as they are connected to the first tree they are exempt from orla, for they are still considered its continuation. But if the branch connecting the original tree to the havrakha was cut, or this part withered, the havrakha becomes obligated in orla and one must begin to count three years for it.

If new suckers (sorim) came up from under the ground, even though they came up from the root system of the old tree, as long as this is not recognizable, for example where they emerged at a significant distance from the tree, they have the law of a new tree that is obligated in orla (Bava Metzia 119a; Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 10:19). However, if the suckers grew close to the old tree, so that it is recognizable that they are part of it and emerged from its trunk below the ground, there is room to say that according to halakha they do not have the law of orla, since they are part of the old tree. However, since many are stringent in this, considering these suckers too as a new tree, it is proper to be stringent.8

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Pots and Nurseries
sections.html:
A tree growing inside a house is obligated in orla, for the main thing regarding the obligation of orla is that the tree be planted in the ground, and the roof above it does not exempt it from orla. Likewise, a tree planted on the roof of a house is obligated in orla; and although air separates the roof from the ground, since the roof itself is connected to the ground through the walls, the roof itself is considered part of the ground and the tree upon it is considered as planted in the ground (SA 294:26).

One who plants a seedling in a perforated pot is considered as planting in the ground, and begins to count the years of orla. Likewise, one who plants a tree in an unperforated earthenware pot – the tree is considered as planted in the ground and is obligated in orla, for since its roots can break through the earthenware, even before they break through it they are considered as drawing from the ground. And some say that even a tree growing in a metal pot is obligated in orla, even though it is clear that the roots cannot penetrate it.9

Following the development of agriculture, with the improvement of fertilizing and irrigation, many trees are able to yield many fruits in the third year. And since the fruits are forbidden for benefit, and there is a loss in the trees occupying expensive land for nothing, a solution was found for this: to keep the trees for about two years in nurseries inside perforated plastic pots, where they occupy a small space and the cost of maintaining them is low, and in the third year to transfer them to the ground, so that they will strengthen in the soil and yield many fruits in the fourth year, whose fruits are permitted.

In practice, since one takes into account the opinion of those who hold that an unperforated plastic pot is exempt from orla, in order that the time the plantings spend in the pots be counted toward the three years of orla according to all opinions, one must be careful about two things: 1) That there be in the pot a hole the size of a small root, by means of which it will be considered connected to the ground; and it is customary to be stringent that the hole be 2.5 cm in diameter.10 2) When transferring the seedling from the pot to the ground, the clod around the roots must not fall apart. After the fact, even if most of it fell apart, as long as its roots have a clod of earth in which they are rooted, it can still survive by means of it, and there is no need to count three years for it again. But if almost the entire clod fell apart, to the point that there is concern that without placing it in the ground, even with irrigating and tending the clod, it could not survive for 14 days, one must count three years of orla for it from the beginning.11

sections.title: Defining the Trees Obligated in Orla
sections.html:
The mitzva of orla applies to fruit trees and not to vegetables, and even vegetables that grow on perennial bushes are exempt from orla. The main difference between a tree and a perennial vegetable is that the stem of a perennial vegetable withers each year and grows again the next year from its roots, whereas the trunk of a tree, with its roots, remains and grows stronger from year to year, and from it branches and fruits continue to grow each year. According to this the blessing over eating the fruit is also determined, 'Ha-etz' or 'Ha-adama'. Therefore one recites 'Ha-adama' over a banana; and although it grows to a height of about four meters and looks like a tree, since each year its trunk withers and its roots wilt and it grows again from its bulb, it is considered a vegetable (Berakhot 40a; following the Ge'onim; SA and Rema OḤ 203:2-3; Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 8:2).12

Regarding eggplants and peppers a question arose, since their stem remains from year to year. However, in practice they do not have the law of orla, for they are entirely different from a tree: they give fruit already in the first year, and in the second year their fruits diminish in quantity and quality, and they do not give fruit for more than three years. And as we learned in the Torah, a tree gives fruit for at least five years, and in the merit of keeping the mitzva of orla its fruits increase and improve in the fifth year, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23-25): "And when you come into the land and plant any tree for food, you shall treat its fruit as forbidden; three years it shall be forbidden to you, it shall not be eaten. And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, for giving praise to the Lord. And in the fifth year you may eat its fruit, so that it may increase its yield for you; I am the Lord your God." And as the Sages said: "This mitzva that you keep will serve to increase its yield for you, for as its reward I will bless for you the fruits of the planting. Rabbi Akiva used to say: The Torah spoke in response to the evil inclination, so that a person should not say, 'Behold, for four years I trouble myself over it for nothing'; therefore it is stated: 'so that it may increase its yield for you; I am the Lord' – I am the Lord who promises this and am faithful to keep My promise" (Rashi, based on Torat Kohanim there). And so the Ramban explains (there), that the fruits growing in the third year are few and poor, and only in the fourth year do they become good and fit to be brought before God, as in the mitzva of neta revai.

Accordingly, there is also no law of orla in papaya and passion fruit, since they give fruit already in the first year, and by the fifth year their fruits diminish, and many of them also do not survive for five years. True, some are stringent in this, but the main view follows those who permit. Likewise, there is no law of orla in raspberries and blackberries [?] of all their kinds, as explained in the note.13

sections.title: One Who Plants Not for the Sake of Fruit
sections.html:
One who plants a fruit tree not for the sake of its fruit but for the sake of its timber or so that it will serve as a fence – the fruits growing on it do not have the law of orla, since it is not considered a food tree, whereas the mitzva of orla applies only to a food tree, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23): "and plant any tree for food – you shall treat its fruit as forbidden." However, the Sages said that one may be lenient in this on condition that it is recognizable that the tree is planted there not for the sake of eating its fruit; for example, the trees are very dense, so that it is recognizable that they were planted in order to use their wood for burning; or one prunes its branches in a way that causes them to thicken, so that it is recognizable that the tree was planted in order to use its branches as planks for building; or by the precise location of the trees' planting it is recognizable that they were planted to serve as a fence for the courtyard. And even if one intended that only one side of the tree would serve as a fence while its other side would be for growing fruit, the fence side is exempt from orla and the fruit side is obligated in orla (Mishna and Yerushalmi, Orla 1:1; SA 294:23). And if he wishes to eat the permitted fruits, he should separate terumot and ma'asrot from them without a blessing (see Yerushalmi Orla 1:1). And if he planted the tree both for a fence or timber and for fruit, its fruits have the law of orla.

Those who plant trees for ornament, such as olive trees, the fruits do not have the law of orla. However, a doubt arose regarding trees that were planted for ornament, but where the beauty of their fruits is also desired, such as pomegranates and date palms. And since the law of orla is by Torah law, one must be stringent in the doubt. Only when it is clear that they did not intend the beauty of the fruits do they not have the law of orla.

sections.title: Neta Revai
sections.html:
The fruits growing on the trees in the fourth year are holy, and it is a mitzva to eat them in purity in Jerusalem, like the law of ma'aser sheni (below 7:9-10). If he wishes, the owner of the fruits may redeem the fruits with money, bring the money up to Jerusalem, buy food with it and eat it in purity. Since the fruits of neta revai are holy, there is no mitzva to leave from them leket, shikheḥa and pe'a for the poor, and there is no mitzva to separate terumot and ma'asrot from them (Mishna and Yerushalmi, Ma'aser Sheni 5:3-4; Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:1-4).

Nowadays, when we cannot bring the fruits of the fourth year up to Jerusalem and eat them in purity, we redeem all the fruits with money or something of monetary value, and thereby permit the fruits to be eaten. And although they are many fruits, since we are forbidden to eat them nowadays, they have no value at all; but it is impossible to perform an act of redemption with less than the value of a peruta, and therefore one redeems all the fruits onto a coin worth at least a peruta or onto a food worth a peruta. Before the redemption one recites: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of revai," and says: "All these fruits are redeemed with this peruta," or "with this food that is worth a peruta." And the peruta or the food that became sanctified through the redemption is destroyed, so that people will not stumble and benefit from it (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 10:16-17). All the details of these laws will be explained below in the laws of the redemption of ma'aser sheni (below 10:6-8).14

The laws of orla and neta revai also apply to the fruits of the Sabbatical year: if the fruits are in the first three years of the tree – they are orla and forbidden to eat; and if they are in the fourth year – anyone is permitted to pick them, but they must be eaten in Jerusalem, and nowadays they must be deconsecrated onto a peruta. Owners of fields must mark the trees in the Sabbatical year, so that those who come to the field will be careful with them when they are orla, and will know to redeem them when they are neta revai. After their redemption one must be careful to finish eating them by the time of bi'ur (removal), and if one did not do so, one must remove them in the way that the other fruits of the Sabbatical year must be removed (Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:7; Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 4:5).

The poskim disagree regarding 'neta revai' outside the Land. Some say that since it is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai that the mitzva of orla applies outside the Land, the mitzva of neta revai also applies outside the Land, for orla and neta revai depend on each other (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Ri the Elder). And some say that the law of neta revai is like the law of ma'aser sheni, which applies only in the Land of Israel (Rambam). Ideally it is good to fulfill all opinions and to redeem neta revai outside the Land without a blessing (Shakh 294:17). And one who wishes to be lenient and not redeem – may do so, for just as one is lenient in doubtful orla outside the Land, so the halakha follows the lenient opinion in doubtful neta revai.15

sections.title: Doubts Concerning Orla
sections.html:
Orla fruits that became mixed with ordinary fruits of the same kind: as long as the kosher fruits are not two hundred times the orla, the entire mixture is forbidden. For so the Sages established: teruma, which is forbidden to eat and permitted for benefit, is nullified in one hundred, whereas orla and kilayim, which are forbidden to eat and for benefit, are nullified in two hundred (Mishna Orla 2:1).

All this is when the orla fruits became mixed in among the permitted fruits. But if a doubt arose regarding certain fruits that a person bought, whether they are orla or not, the law depends on the question of where the doubt arose. If the fruits were bought in the orchard or near the orchard, even though most orchards and trees are not orla, since the tree or the orchard has a fixed place, the orla fruits are not nullified, according to the rule: "Kol kavua ke-meḥtza al meḥtza dami" (anything fixed is considered as half and half), and the fruits are forbidden. But if the fruits were bought after they had been separated from their fixed place and brought to the market or to the stores, then it is an ordinary doubt, and one follows the majority, according to the rule: "Kol de-parish me-ruba parish" (whatever separates is considered as separating from the majority).

However, all this is after the fact, regarding a person who bought fruits and does not know what their status is, or who is in a place where there are no stores with a kashrut certificate and to reach such a store he would have to go to great trouble. But if there is a store there with a kashrut certificate, he must avoid the doubt and buy there. And even if he knows that it is a very remote doubt, because the percentage of orla in these fruits or in this area is extremely low, when possible one is obligated to avoid the doubt. In addition, it is a mitzva to strengthen those who are meticulous about kashrut. Furthermore, when there is a kashrut certificate, terumot and ma'asrot are also separated properly.16
